# A sharp joint-row budget for a simplex cap circuit in every dimension

This note is an ordinary geometric input for finite mixed cap certificates.
It proves a sharp joint inequality, not an arbitrary-body inequality or a
promotion across lattice-free facets. In dimension two it recovers the
previously proved Lorentz family. No lattice parity inference is made.

## 1. Actual cap data and the balanced matrix

Let d>=2 and m=d+1. Let K be a d-dimensional simplex, let y belong to
its interior, and let v_1,...,v_m be nonzero spanning normals satisfying
sum v_i=0. Suppose the halfspace v_i.(x-y)>=0 isolates vertex P_i:

    v_i.(P_i-y)>0,       v_i.(P_j-y)<0 for j!=i.

Put H=sum_i v_i.(P_i-y)>0 and define

    a_i=v_i.(P_i-y)/H,
    b_ij=-v_i.(P_j-y)/H       (i!=j).

Then a_i>0, b_ij>0, sum a_i=1, and the normal balance gives the
column identities

    sum_(i!=j) b_ij=a_j.                                  (1)

The cap at P_i is a simplex whose edge fractions are
a_i/(a_i+b_ij). Consequently its volume fraction q_i and the quantities
f_i,g_i are

    q_i=a_i^d/product_(j!=i)(a_i+b_ij),
    f_i=d a_i/q_i^(1/d)
       =d[product_(j!=i)(a_i+b_ij)]^(1/d),
    g_i=d a_i+sum_(j!=i)b_ij.                             (2)

In particular sum g_i=d+1. The normalized section measure of the cut,
meaning its (d-1)-volume divided by ||v_i||, is

    sigma_i=d |K| q_i/(H a_i).

Thus normalized inverse-section weights are proportional to
f_i/q_i^((d-1)/d). This identity retains the actual common height H.

## 2. Elementary row deficit, kept separate from the joint theorem

The arithmetic-geometric mean inequality gives f_i<=g_i and hence

    F:=sum_i f_i<=d+1.                                   (3)

There is also an explicit nonnegative row-variance budget:

    d+1-F >= (1/d) sum_i sum_(j<k; j,k!=i)
       [sqrt(a_i+b_ij)-sqrt(a_i+b_ik)]^2.                 (4)

Indeed for positive x_1,...,x_d, AM--GM applied to their square roots
gives (product x)^(1/d)<=(sum sqrt x/d)^2. Therefore

    sum x-d(product x)^(1/d)
      >=sum x-(sum sqrt x)^2/d
       =(1/d)sum_(j<k)(sqrt x_j-sqrt x_k)^2.

Apply this independently to each row and sum. Inequality (4) alone
does not express the joint column constraint needed below.

## 3. The sharp joint inequality

**Theorem.** Every matrix satisfying the positive data and (1), and
therefore every actual cap configuration in Section 1, satisfies for
each i

    f_i+(d-1)[(sum_(j!=i) f_j)/d]^(d/(d-1))<=d.           (5)

For d=2 this is exactly

    f_i+(f_j+f_k)^2/4<=2.

**Proof.** Fix i. Average the balanced matrix over all simultaneous
permutations of its row and column indices that fix i. This averaging
preserves positivity, sum a=1 and every column identity (1). Write

    A=a_i,
    B=(1/d)sum_(j!=i)b_ij,
    t=(1-A)/d,
    C=(t-B)/(d-1).

The averaged matrix has selected diagonal A, selected off-diagonal
entries B, other diagonals t, entries from the other rows into column i
equal to A/d, and all remaining off-diagonal entries equal to C. All
of A,B,t,C are positive.

The function geometric mean is concave on the positive orthant. For
completeness, it has the linear-infimum representation

    (product x_j)^(1/d)
       =inf_{r_j>0, product r_j=1} (sum r_j x_j)/d.

AM--GM proves the lower bound, and r_j=(product x)^(1/d)/x_j gives
equality. An infimum of linear functions is concave, proving the
assertion without a smoothness assumption.

Each f_j is d times that concave function of the corresponding d
channels a_j+b_jk. Concavity applied to the selected row gives

    f_i<=bar f_i=d(A+B)=g_i.

Concavity at each other row, followed by summation, gives

    g:=sum_(j!=i) f_j <=bar g:=sum_(j!=i) bar f_j.

The sum on the right of each pre-averaging permuted matrix is the same
g, so no individual monotonicity of the original other rows is assumed.
In an averaged other row, its channel toward i is

    t+A/d=1/d,

and its d-1 other channels are

    t+C=(1-A-B)/(d-1).

It follows exactly that

    bar g=d[(d-bar f_i)/(d-1)]^((d-1)/d).                (6)

Here bar f_i<d, since B<(1-A)/d and A<1. The right side of (6) is a
strictly decreasing function of bar f_i. Since bar f_i>=f_i and
g<=bar g, raising to the positive power d/(d-1) proves (5). QED.

The proof averages algebraic data solely to prove the inequality. It
does not claim that independent row alterations preserve the original
mixed fibers, lattice, cap budgets or selected source.

## 4. Equality and an exact deficit decomposition

Let p=d/(d-1), and retain bar f_i and bar g from the preceding proof.
There is the exact decomposition

    d-f_i-(d-1)(g/d)^p
      =(bar f_i-f_i)
       +(d-1)[(bar g/d)^p-(g/d)^p].                      (7)

Both terms are nonnegative. Thus equality in (5) requires and is
equivalent to equality in BOTH averaging steps, not just an AM--GM
equality in the selected row.

For clarity, the full positive-matrix equality criterion is as follows.
There are A>0 and B>0 with

    a_i=A, b_ij=B for j!=i,
    Q=(1-A-B)/(d-1)>0,

such that for every j!=i

    a_j+b_ji=1/d,
    a_j+b_jk=Q       for k!=i,j.                         (8)

The a_j need not be equal; positivity of the displayed b's remains
part of the matrix hypotheses.

To prove necessity, equality for the selected row implies its channel
vector is invariant under every coordinate permutation up to a positive
factor. Equal coordinate sums make that factor one, so b_ij=B. Equality
in the other averaged rows implies all their permuted channel vectors
are proportional. This equality condition follows directly from the
linear-infimum proof: one supporting linear form must be optimal at
every averaged positive vector, forcing proportional vectors.

Permuting the other d-1 columns while fixing a row j shows that all its
channels not pointing to i are a common value Q_j (for d=2 there is
only one such channel). The ratio P_j/Q_j, where P_j=a_j+b_ji, is
independent of j by the proportionality across rows. Now column j in
(1), for j!=i, gives

    a_j=B+sum_(l!=i,j)(Q_l-a_l),

or Q_j=B+sum_(l!=i)Q_l-1+A. Hence every Q_j has the same value Q and
then every P_j is the same P. Column i gives
A=sum_(j!=i)(P-a_j)=dP-1+A, so P=1/d. The preceding identity for Q
gives Q=(1-A-B)/(d-1). This proves (8). Conversely (8) makes all the
averaged channel vectors identical, so equality follows.

## 5. Every interior point of the joint frontier is actual and sharp

Fix any x in (0,d). Choose

    max(0,(x-1)/(d-1)) < A < x/d,
    B=x/d-A,
    t=(1-A)/d,
    C=(t-B)/(d-1).

All four quantities are positive. In R^d take the normals e_1,...,e_d
and v_0=-sum e_j, and define a simplex with source zero and vertices

    P_0=-(A/d) 1,
    P_j=(t+C)e_j-C 1       (j=1,...,d).

Their balanced evaluation matrix is exactly the symmetric matrix in
Section 3. The d edge differences P_j-P_0 form a matrix with eigenvalues
t+C on the sum-zero subspace and A+B on the all-ones direction; both
are positive. Hence these vertices are affinely independent. Moreover
zero has positive barycentric weights

    alpha_0=B/(A+B),
    alpha_j=A/[d(A+B)]       (j=1,...,d),

so the source lies in the simplex interior. Every cap isolates the
claimed strict vertex. Formula (2) gives

    f_0=x,
    sum_(j=1)^d f_j
      =d[(d-x)/(d-1)]^((d-1)/d).

Thus equality in (5) is attained by actual simplices for every allowed
selected value x. A stronger universal joint frontier is impossible.

## 6. Scope in a mixed certificate

Any group of d+1 ambient halfspaces whose continuous normals form a
positive circuit may first have its inequalities rescaled by their
positive circuit coefficients. At a source in a simplex fiber, if the
traces isolate distinct strict vertices, the preceding theorem applies
to that group's actual continuous cap fractions after translation of
the source. The numerical integer coefficients are multiplied by the
same positive factors; the ambient halfspaces and all their fiber
traces remain unchanged.

This supplies a sharp local joint-row restriction in arbitrary d and
at arbitrary integer dimension n. It does not imply that other fiber
volumes obey the same rows, that the traces isolate vertices for an
arbitrary convex fiber, or that these inequalities add over at most
2^n lattice-free facets with the sharp global budget. Those arithmetic
and cross-fiber steps remain separate.

For d=1 the row has one channel and (1) gives f_1=f_2=1. The exponent
d/(d-1) is not used. Boundary vertex incidences were excluded in the
theorem and have not been discarded by an approximation argument.
